title: Practice Before Performance: Two Simple Ways to Turn Advice Into Employee Skills
author: Kurt Mueller
source: kurtmueller.substack.com (Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership), October 2, 2026
summary: Kurt Mueller draws on his years at Disney to argue that scripts and rehearsals are two underused leadership development tools. His central claim is that explaining a principle or handing over a checklist does not make someone ready to perform, because knowing what to do differs from being able to do it when the moment arrives. A script turns a vague expectation such as "be proactive" into concrete language an employee can actually practice, for example an early heads-up message to a stakeholder when a delivery will slip. A rehearsal then lets the leader play a skeptical stakeholder, challenge a first-time presenter, and debrief with questions about what worked and what caught them off guard. He extends the idea to role plays, simulations and short "what would you say next?" exercises in team meetings. The payoff is observable practice before the stakes are high, which also gives team members the chance to stumble and adjust safely.
points: A script converts a vague expectation into practicable language, so the leader coaches a specific sentence rather than a trait such as "be more proactive."
The script is a starting point, not something to memorize; the aim is for the employee to make the language their own once the skill becomes natural.
A fifteen-minute rehearsal in which the leader plays a challenging stakeholder is more revealing than reviewing slides and surfaces uncertainty before the real meeting.
Rehearsals can be escalated with added objections, time pressure or surprise questions, and debriefed with four simple questions about what worked and what to change.
The deeper benefit is observable practice: leaders see whether a skill is present instead of assuming it, and employees get a low-stakes chance to fail and adjust.
quotes: Because knowing what you should do is very different from being ready to do it when the situation arrives.
Now you’ve converted a vague expectation—be proactive—into something the employee can actually practice. The objective isn’t memorization.
Theater doesn’t move directly from receiving the script to opening night. There are rehearsals.
Each provides an opportunity to practice, receive feedback, make adjustments and increase readiness before the consequences become real.
Instead of simply reviewing their slides, conduct a 15-minute rehearsal.
Instead of assuming someone is ready because you’ve explained what good performance looks like, you get to see the skill being used before the stakes are high.
The goal isn’t perfect performance during practice. It’s greater readiness when the real situation arrives.
